title: IELTS Academic Writing — Practice Test 3
topics: How recycled paper is produced from waste paper
The decline in people entering skilled manual trades

task1.prompt:
The diagram below shows how recycled paper is produced from waste paper collected from homes and businesses.

Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.

visual.title: Production of recycled paper from collected waste paper

stages.name: Collection
stages.description: Waste paper and cardboard are collected from household recycling bins and from offices and shops, then delivered by lorry to a sorting depot.

stages.name: Sorting
stages.description: At the depot the paper is sorted by grade (newsprint, office paper, cardboard). Plastic, metal and heavily soiled paper are removed by hand and by magnets, and the sorted paper is pressed into bales.

stages.name: Pulping
stages.description: At the paper mill the bales are fed into a large vat called a pulper, where they are mixed with warm water and chemicals and agitated until the paper breaks down into a thick fibrous slurry called pulp.

stages.name: Screening
stages.description: The pulp passes through a series of screens with progressively smaller holes. Staples, glue, tape and fragments of plastic are trapped and removed, while the fibres pass through.

stages.name: De-inking
stages.description: Air is bubbled through the pulp in a flotation tank. Ink particles attach to the bubbles, rise to the surface as a foam and are skimmed off. Some pulp is then washed to remove any remaining ink.

stages.name: Refining and bleaching
stages.description: The clean pulp is beaten to make the fibres more flexible and, if white paper is required, it is lightly bleached with hydrogen peroxide rather than chlorine.

stages.name: Paper making
stages.description: The pulp, now more than 99% water, is sprayed onto a fast-moving wire mesh. Water drains through the mesh, leaving a continuous sheet of wet fibres.

stages.name: Pressing and drying
stages.description: The sheet passes between heavy rollers that squeeze out more water, and then over a series of heated cylinders that dry it completely.

stages.name: Finishing and distribution
stages.description: The dry paper is wound onto large reels, cut to size and packaged before being sent to printers, packaging firms and shops.

task2.prompt:
In many developed countries, fewer young people are choosing to train for skilled manual trades such as plumbing, electrical work and construction, even though these jobs are in high demand and often well paid.

What are the causes of this? What measures could be taken to address it?

ta: Gives a clear overview that describes the process as a whole: a linear sequence of nine stages that begins with collection and sorting, moves through several cleaning stages at the mill, and ends with a finished reel of paper.

Covers every stage without omitting the less obvious ones — in particular the two separate cleaning steps (screening removes solid contaminants; de-inking removes ink) — while giving more space to the stages that need explanation than to the simple ones.
Identifies the natural groupings: preparation (stages 1–2), turning paper into clean pulp (3–6), and turning pulp back into paper (7–9).
Describes, rather than evaluates: no comments on whether recycling is worthwhile or how the process could be improved.
cc: Sequences the stages with varied markers ("once", "at this point", "having been screened", "the final stage") rather than "Firstly… Secondly… Thirdly" for nine steps.
Paragraphs by phase (preparation / pulping and cleaning / sheet formation and finishing) so the report has shape instead of one long list.
Uses referencing to carry material through the process ("the resulting slurry", "this sheet", "the pulp") so that each sentence connects to the previous one.
lr: Uses the process vocabulary from the diagram accurately and paraphrases where possible: bales, pulper, slurry, screened, contaminants, flotation, skimmed off, bleached, mesh, reels.
Controls verbs of transformation: broken down into, converted into, separated from, drained through, wound onto.
Avoids over-reliance on the diagram's exact wording by re-expressing it ("heavily soiled paper is removed" → "contaminated material is discarded").
gra: Uses the present simple passive consistently and accurately ("is sorted", "are pressed into bales", "is sprayed onto"), which is the natural voice for a man-made process.
Varies sentence openings with participle and time clauses ("After being screened, the pulp…", "Once the ink has been removed…").
Punctuates sequences correctly and avoids comma splices when linking consecutive stages; errors are rare.

ta: Answers both questions with comparable depth: at least one full paragraph on causes and one on measures, rather than a long diagnosis followed by a single sentence of solutions.

Identifies specific, plausible causes — the social status of university degrees, school careers advice that favours academic routes, the physical demands and perceived insecurity of trade work, the cost and length of apprenticeships — rather than "young people are lazy".
Proposes measures that match the causes identified (e.g. if status is a cause, the measure addresses status), and shows who would implement them: governments, schools, employers or trade bodies.
Engages with the tension in the prompt — these jobs are well paid and in demand, yet unattractive — instead of ignoring it.
cc: A clear structure in which causes and solutions are kept in separate paragraphs (or clearly signposted within one), each with a topic sentence.
Ideas progress logically; each solution is visibly linked back to the cause it addresses ("to counter this perception…").
Cohesion through referencing and sequencing ("this imbalance", "such schemes", "a second measure"), not a linker at the start of every sentence.
lr: Uses precise vocabulary for the topic: vocational, apprenticeship, skills shortage, stigma, parity of esteem, earning potential, ageing workforce, career progression.
Paraphrases the prompt ("skilled manual trades" → "vocational occupations", "hands-on professions") rather than copying it.
Uses collocations naturally ("raise the profile of", "bridge the skills gap", "a shortage of qualified tradespeople") without forced rare words.
gra: A range of complex structures under control: cause-and-effect forms ("This has led to…", "As a result of…"), conditionals for proposals ("If schools were to…"), and relative clauses.
Accurate modal verbs for recommendations ("should", "could", "would need to") and hedged claims about causes ("appears to", "tends to").
Punctuation handles lists of causes and subordinate clauses correctly; errors are rare and never impede meaning.

traps.title: Merging screening and de-inking
traps.detail: Stages 4 and 5 are different cleaning operations: screening removes solid contaminants (staples, tape, plastic) with sieves; de-inking removes ink using air bubbles in a flotation tank. Writing "the pulp is cleaned" for both loses a key feature.

traps.title: No overview for a process
traps.detail: Candidates often think an overview is only for graphs. For a process, state how many stages there are, where it begins and ends, and that it is linear (not cyclical) before describing the steps.

traps.title: Copying the diagram's labels word for word
traps.detail: Lifting every description unchanged earns little credit for Lexical Resource. Paraphrase where you can ("agitated until the paper breaks down" → "stirred until the fibres separate") while keeping technical terms such as pulper and flotation.

traps.title: Slipping out of the passive
traps.detail: Switching to "they collect the paper" or "we sort it" introduces an unknown agent. Keep the present simple passive throughout, except where the material itself acts ("water drains through the mesh").

traps.title: Adding your own chemistry
traps.detail: Explaining how hydrogen peroxide works or why chlorine is avoided is outside the diagram. Report only what is shown.

traps.title: Answering only the first question
traps.detail: This is a two-question task. An essay that gives three causes and then a one-line "governments should promote these jobs" has not fully addressed the task and is capped at Band 6 for Task Response.

traps.title: Generic solutions with no owner
traps.detail: "Awareness should be raised" is not a measure. Say who does what: schools inviting tradespeople to careers days, employers paying apprentices a living wage, governments offering tax relief to firms that train.

traps.title: Drifting into automation or immigration
traps.detail: The question is about why young people in developed countries are not choosing these trades. Essays about robots replacing builders or about migrant labour filling the gap are answering a different question.
